questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): Replication is discontinuous on the template strand that has 5'→3' polarity.
Reason (R): DNA-dependent DNA polymerases catalyse polymerisation only in one direction, that is 5'→3'.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Continuous and discontinuous synthesis at the replication fork
solution.explanation: A new strand grows only 5'→3', so it must run antiparallel to its template. On the template with 3'→5' polarity the new strand grows towards the fork, continuously. On the template with 5'→3' polarity it can only be made in short pieces away from the fork, which are joined by DNA ligase. The one-direction activity of DNA polymerase (R) is exactly why A happens.
steps: Polymerase works only 5'→3' → one strand must be made in fragments → R explains A
solution.why_others_wrong: Students who remember 'the 3'→5' template is continuous' sometimes mark A false; the question names the other template.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Molecular Basis of Inheritance', replication: the machinery and the enzymes
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

Given below are two statements:

Statement I: DNA fingerprinting involves identifying differences in some specific regions of the DNA sequence called repetitive DNA.
Statement II: Satellite DNA sequences normally code for proteins, which is why they differ between individuals.

(b) Rhizobium fixes atmospheric nitrogen only while living free in the soil, without forming root nodules.
(c) Anabaena, Nostoc and Oscillatoria are cyanobacteria that can fix atmospheric nitrogen.
(d) Baculoviruses of the genus Nucleopolyhedrovirus are broad-spectrum insecticides that also harm non-target insects.
(e) Trichoderma species are free-living fungi that act as biocontrol agents against several plant pathogens.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.explanation: Glomus forms mycorrhiza and helps phosphorus uptake. Rhizobium fixes nitrogen symbiotically in root nodules of legumes; Azospirillum and Azotobacter are the free-living fixers. Cyanobacteria fix nitrogen, important in paddy fields. Baculoviruses (Nucleopolyhedrovirus) are species-specific, narrow-spectrum insecticides with no negative effect on non-target insects, so they suit IPM. Trichoderma is a free-living fungal biocontrol agent.
steps: (b) False: Rhizobium is symbiotic in root nodules
(d) False: baculoviruses are narrow-spectrum and spare non-target insects
solution.why_others_wrong: Every option except B includes (b) or (d), each of which reverses an NCERT statement.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Microbes in Human Welfare', microbes as biocontrol agents; microbes as biofertilisers
solution.final_answer: Option B: (a), (c) and (e) only

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: Wine and beer are produced by distilling the fermented broth, whereas whisky, brandy and rum are produced without distillation.
Statement II: Statins produced by Monascus purpureus lower blood cholesterol by competitively inhibiting the enzyme responsible for cholesterol synthesis.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.explanation: Wine and beer are produced without distillation, while whisky, brandy and rum are made by distilling the fermented broth; Statement I swaps the two groups. Statins from Monascus purpureus act as competitive inhibitors of the enzyme responsible for cholesterol synthesis, so Statement II is true.
solution.why_others_wrong: Statement I keeps the right beverages but reverses the process, a common NEET trap.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Microbes in Human Welfare', microbes in industrial products: fermented beverages; bioactive molecules
solution.final_answer: Option D: Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text: Which of the following statements about microbes in household products is correct?

options.text: Lactic acid bacteria convert milk to curd by producing ethyl alcohol
In our stomach, lactic acid bacteria are harmful because they produce toxins
Lactic acid bacteria convert milk to curd and also increase its vitamin B₁₂ content
Roquefort cheese is ripened by growing a specific bacterium on it

solution.explanation: LAB grow in milk and produce acids that coagulate and partially digest the milk proteins, forming curd. They also improve its nutritional quality by increasing vitamin B₁₂. In our stomach, LAB play a beneficial role in checking disease-causing microbes. Roquefort cheese is ripened by growing a specific fungus on it.
steps: Curd: acid (lactic) production by LAB, plus more vitamin B₁₂ → correct
solution.why_others_wrong: LAB produce acid, not alcohol; they are beneficial in the gut; Roquefort ripening uses a fungus.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Microbes in Human Welfare', microbes in household products
solution.final_answer: Option C: Lactic acid bacteria convert milk to curd and also increase its vitamin B₁₂ content

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text: An interaction in which one species benefits and the other is neither harmed nor benefited is called:

solution.explanation: Interactions are classified by the effect on each species: mutualism (+, +), competition (−, −), predation and parasitism (+, −), commensalism (+, 0) and amensalism (−, 0).
solution.why_others_wrong: Amensalism is (−, 0), mutualism (+, +) and competition (−, −).
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Organisms and Populations', population interactions
solution.final_answer: Option B: Commensalism

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text: In the logistic growth equation dN/dt = rN[(K − N)/K], the symbol K stands for:

options.text: The intrinsic rate of natural increase
The population density at time t
The number of births per unit time
The carrying capacity of the habitat

solution.explanation: In a habitat with limited resources, the population grows until it reaches the maximum the habitat can support. This limit is the carrying capacity, K. N is the population density at time t and r is the intrinsic rate of natural increase.
steps: N = population density at time t
r = intrinsic rate of natural increase
solution.why_others_wrong: r, N and births are separate terms; K is the upper limit set by resources.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Organisms and Populations', population growth: logistic growth
solution.final_answer: Option D: The carrying capacity of the habitat

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text: An age pyramid with a broad base, i.e. a large proportion of pre-reproductive individuals, indicates a population that is:

options.text: At its carrying capacity and about to crash

solution.explanation: Plotting pre-reproductive, reproductive and post-reproductive individuals gives an age pyramid. A broad base (many young individuals) shows a growing population, a bell shape a stable one, and a narrow base a declining one.
solution.why_others_wrong: A declining population has a narrow base; a stable one is bell-shaped.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Organisms and Populations', population attributes
solution.final_answer: Option C: Expanding (growing)

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text: The Mediterranean orchid Ophrys gets pollinated by a species of bee through:

options.text: Offering large amounts of nectar as a reward
Sexual deceit: one petal resembles the female bee and the male bee 'pseudocopulates' with the flower
Providing a site for the bee to lay its eggs
Trapping the bee inside the flower until pollination is complete

solution.explanation: One petal of the Ophrys flower looks like a female bee in size, colour and markings. The male bee tries to mate with it ('pseudocopulation') and is dusted with pollen, which it transfers to another flower. If the female bee's colour pattern changes slightly in evolution, pollination success falls unless the orchid flower co-evolves.
steps: Petal mimics female bee → male bee pseudocopulates → pollen transferred
solution.why_others_wrong: Nectar is a common floral reward, but not Ophrys's strategy. Egg-laying in the flower describes the fig–wasp and Yucca–moth relationships.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Organisms and Populations', population interactions: mutualism
solution.final_answer: Option B: Sexual deceit: one petal resembles the female bee and the male bee 'pseudocopulates' with the flower

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text: A laboratory population of 250 fruit flies produced 50 offspring and lost 25 individuals to death during one week. The birth rate and death rate of this population, per individual per week, are respectively:

solution.concept: Birth rate and death rate as per capita rates
solution.explanation: Birth and death rates are expressed per individual of the population at the start of the period, i.e. as rates relative to the members of the population.
steps: Birth rate = 50 / 250 = 0.2 offspring per fly per week
Death rate = 25 / 250 = 0.1 death per fly per week
solution.why_others_wrong: 50 and 25 are absolute numbers, not rates per individual. 0.1 and 0.2 swap the two rates. 0.18 and 0.09 divide by the population at the end of the week (275).
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Organisms and Populations', population attributes
solution.final_answer: Option A: 0.2 and 0.1

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): The monarch butterfly is highly distasteful to its predators, such as birds.
Reason (R): During its caterpillar stage, the monarch butterfly feeds on a poisonous weed and acquires a special chemical from it.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.explanation: Prey species have evolved defences against predation. The monarch butterfly acquires a chemical from a poisonous weed it eats as a caterpillar; this chemical makes the adult distasteful to birds. R gives the cause of A.
steps: Chemical from the weed → distasteful → R explains A
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Organisms and Populations', population interactions: predation
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text:
Match List-I (example) with List-II (interaction).

List-I:
A. Cuscuta growing on hedge plants
B. An orchid growing as an epiphyte on a mango branch
C. Lichens
D. Balanus and Chthamalus on the rocky sea coasts of Scotland

List-II:
I. Mutualism
II. Competition
III. Commensalism
IV. Parasitism

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.explanation: Each example is an NCERT illustration of one interaction.
steps: Cuscuta: a parasitic plant without chlorophyll that takes nutrition from the host → parasitism (A-IV)
Epiphytic orchid on mango: orchid benefits, mango unaffected → commensalism (B-III)
Lichen: fungus and photosynthesising alga or cyanobacterium both benefit → mutualism (C-I)
Connell's barnacles: the larger Balanus excludes Chthamalus from the intertidal zone → competition (D-II)
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Organisms and Populations', population interactions
solution.final_answer: Option D: A-IV, B-III, C-I, D-II

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: Exponential growth occurs when resources in the habitat are limited, and it gives an S-shaped curve.
Statement II: A population growing in a habitat with limited resources shows an initial lag phase, followed by phases of acceleration and deceleration, and finally an asymptote when the population density reaches the carrying capacity.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.explanation: Exponential growth happens when resources are unlimited; plotting N against time gives a J-shaped curve. With limited resources, growth is logistic: lag, acceleration, deceleration and an asymptote at K, giving a sigmoid (S-shaped) curve.
steps: Statement I: exponential growth needs unlimited resources and gives a J-shaped curve → false
Statement II: correct description of logistic growth → true
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Organisms and Populations', population growth
solution.final_answer: Option D: Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text: For estimating the number of tigers in our national parks and tiger reserves, the tiger census is often based on:

options.text: Number of tigers caught per trap

solution.explanation: Population size need not be counted directly. For tigers, the census in national parks and tiger reserves is often based on pug marks and fecal pellets.
steps: Large, elusive animals → indirect indices → pug marks and fecal pellets
solution.why_others_wrong: Percent cover and biomass suit plants such as Parthenium or a banyan tree; catch per trap is used for fish.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Organisms and Populations', population attributes
solution.final_answer: Option C: Pug marks and fecal pellets

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text: For a population showing logistic growth according to dN/dt = rN[(K − N)/K], which statement is correct?

options.text: The growth rate dN/dt is highest when N equals K
As N approaches K, the growth rate dN/dt approaches zero
When N is very small compared with K, the growth rate is zero
The growth rate is the same at every population density

solution.explanation: The factor (K − N)/K shrinks as N rises. When N is far below K the factor is close to 1 and growth is nearly exponential (rN). When N reaches K, (K − N) = 0, so dN/dt = 0: the population has reached its asymptote.
steps: N ≪ K: (K − N)/K ≈ 1 → dN/dt ≈ rN (fast growth)
solution.why_others_wrong: At N = K the growth rate is zero, not maximum. At small N it is close to rN, not zero. The rate clearly changes with N.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Organisms and Populations', population growth: logistic growth
solution.final_answer: Option B: As N approaches K, the growth rate dN/dt approaches zero

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text:
Which of the following statements about competition and parasitism are correct?

(a) The Abingdon tortoise of the Galapagos Islands became extinct within a decade after goats were introduced, apparently due to the greater browsing efficiency of the goats.
(b) Gause's competitive exclusion principle states that two closely related species competing for the same resources cannot co-exist indefinitely, and the competitively inferior one will be eliminated.
(c) MacArthur found that five closely related species of warblers living on the same tree could not co-exist, and all but one were eliminated.
(d) The cuckoo (koel) lays its eggs in the nest of its host, the crow, which incubates them; this is brood parasitism.
(e) In amensalism, both interacting species are harmed.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Competition, resource partitioning and brood parasitism
solution.explanation: The Abingdon tortoise is NCERT's example of competition. Gause's principle says two closely related species competing for the same resources cannot co-exist indefinitely. MacArthur's warblers avoided competition and co-existed because of behavioural differences in their foraging activities (resource partitioning). The cuckoo is a brood parasite of the crow. In amensalism one species is harmed and the other unaffected.
steps: (c) False: the warblers co-existed by resource partitioning
(e) False: amensalism is (−, 0); both harmed is competition
solution.why_others_wrong: Options A, B and C each contain (c) or (e).
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Organisms and Populations', population interactions: competition; parasitism
solution.final_answer: Option D: (a), (b) and (d) only

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): The human liver fluke depends on two intermediate hosts, a snail and a fish, to complete its life cycle.
Reason (R): Parasites that feed on the external surface of the host organism are called ectoparasites.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Complex life cycles of parasites; ectoparasites
solution.explanation: Many parasites have complex life cycles with one or two intermediate hosts or vectors; the human liver fluke, a trematode, needs a snail and a fish. So A is true. Ectoparasites (lice on humans, ticks on dogs) feed on the external surface of the host, so R is true. But the liver fluke is an endoparasite living inside its host, so the definition of ectoparasites cannot explain its life cycle.
steps: Liver fluke is an endoparasite → R is unrelated to A
solution.why_others_wrong: Option A is the trap: both statements are about parasites and both are true, but R does not explain A.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Organisms and Populations', population interactions: parasitism
solution.final_answer: Option B: Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: The prickly pear cactus introduced into Australia spread rapidly and was brought under control only after a cactus-feeding predator (a moth) from its natural habitat was introduced.
Statement II: Predators help to maintain species diversity in a community by reducing the intensity of competition among competing prey species.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.explanation: An exotic species can spread fast in a new area because its natural predators are absent; the prickly pear in Australia was controlled only after a cactus-feeding moth from its native range was introduced. Predators also keep prey populations in check and so reduce competition among prey species, helping maintain diversity.
steps: Statement I: true (NCERT example; the basis of biological control)
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Organisms and Populations', population interactions: predation
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text: The mass of living material present at a particular trophic level at a particular time is called the:

solution.explanation: Each trophic level has a certain mass of living material at a given time, called the standing crop. It is measured as the biomass of living organisms or as their number per unit area. It is a quantity present at one time, not a rate.
steps: Mass of living material at a trophic level, at one time → standing crop
solution.why_others_wrong: Productivity terms are rates of production of organic matter; detritus is dead organic matter.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Ecosystem', energy flow; ecological pyramids
solution.final_answer: Option C: Standing crop

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text: In an aquatic ecosystem, the primary producers are mainly:

options.text: Phytoplankton, some algae and higher plants

solution.explanation: All organisms depend on producers for food. In terrestrial ecosystems the major producers are herbaceous and woody plants; in aquatic ecosystems they are phytoplankton, some algae and higher plants.
steps: Aquatic producers: phytoplankton, some algae, higher plants
solution.why_others_wrong: Zooplankton and fishes are consumers; fungi and bacteria are decomposers.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Ecosystem', energy flow: producers
solution.final_answer: Option D: Phytoplankton, some algae and higher plants

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text: The detritus food chain (DFC) begins with:

solution.explanation: The grazing food chain starts with producers. The detritus food chain starts with dead organic matter (detritus) and is made up of decomposers, heterotrophs such as fungi and bacteria (saprotrophs), that meet their energy and nutrient needs by degrading it.
solution.why_others_wrong: Living green plants start the grazing food chain; herbivores and carnivores are later links.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Ecosystem', energy flow: food chains
solution.final_answer: Option B: Dead organic matter

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: Decomposition is slower when the detritus is rich in lignin and chitin.
Statement II: A warm and moist environment favours decomposition, whereas low temperature and anaerobiosis inhibit it.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.explanation: Decomposition depends on the chemical composition of the detritus and on climate. Detritus rich in lignin and chitin decomposes slowly; detritus rich in nitrogen and water-soluble substances such as sugars decomposes faster. Temperature and soil moisture regulate the activity of soil microbes: warmth and moisture favour decomposition, while cold and lack of oxygen inhibit it, so organic matter builds up.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Ecosystem', decomposition
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): The pyramid of energy is always upright and can never be inverted.
Reason (R): When energy flows from one trophic level to the next, some energy is always lost as heat at each step.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Why the energy pyramid is always upright
solution.explanation: Each trophic level receives only part of the energy of the level below, because some is lost as heat at every transfer (in line with the second law of thermodynamics). So each higher level always has less energy than the one below, and the energy pyramid cannot be inverted. R explains A.
steps: Loss at every step → each higher level has less energy → always upright
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Ecosystem', ecological pyramids
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text:
Match List-I (step of decomposition) with List-II (what happens).

List-I:
A. Fragmentation
B. Leaching
C. Catabolism
D. Humification

List-II:
I. Bacterial and fungal enzymes degrade detritus into simpler inorganic substances
II. Water-soluble inorganic nutrients go down into the soil horizon and are precipitated as unavailable salts
III. Accumulation of a dark-coloured, amorphous substance that is highly resistant to microbial action
IV. Detritivores such as earthworms break detritus into smaller particles

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.explanation: Decomposition breaks complex organic matter into inorganic substances through fragmentation, leaching, catabolism, humification and mineralisation.
steps: Leaching: soluble nutrients move down and precipitate (B-II)
Catabolism: microbial enzymes → simpler inorganic substances (C-I)
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Ecosystem', decomposition
solution.final_answer: Option C: A-IV, B-II, C-I, D-III

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text:
Which of the following statements about energy flow in ecosystems are correct?

(a) Except for deep-sea hydrothermal ecosystems, the sun is the only source of energy for all ecosystems on Earth.
(b) More than 80 per cent of the incident solar radiation is photosynthetically active radiation (PAR).
(c) Ecosystems are exempt from the second law of thermodynamics.
(d) Plants capture only 2–10 per cent of the PAR, and this small amount sustains the entire living world.
(e) Energy moves in one direction, from producers towards the higher trophic levels, and is lost as heat to the environment.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Energy flow and the laws of thermodynamics
solution.explanation: Of the incident solar radiation, less than 50% is PAR, and plants capture only 2–10% of it. Ecosystems are not exempt from the second law of thermodynamics: they need a constant supply of energy to synthesise molecules and counteract the universal tendency towards disorder. Energy flow is unidirectional, from the sun to producers and then to consumers.
steps: (b) False: less than 50% of incident radiation is PAR
solution.why_others_wrong: Options A, B and C contain (b) or (c), which reverse NCERT statements.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Ecosystem', energy flow
solution.final_answer: Option D: (a), (d) and (e) only

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text: The pyramid of biomass in a sea is generally inverted because:

options.text: Phytoplankton have a greater biomass than all the consumers together
The biomass of fishes far exceeds that of the phytoplankton
Energy increases at each higher trophic level in the sea
Decomposers are placed at the base of the pyramid in the sea

solution.explanation: In the sea, the standing crop of phytoplankton at any moment is small, although they reproduce fast. The biomass of fishes is much larger. Biomass increases at higher trophic levels, so the pyramid of biomass is inverted. The pyramid of energy still remains upright.
solution.why_others_wrong: If phytoplankton had the larger biomass, the pyramid would be upright. Energy never increases upwards. Decomposers are not given a place in ecological pyramids.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Ecosystem', ecological pyramids
solution.final_answer: Option B: The biomass of fishes far exceeds that of the phytoplankton

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text: In the food chain grass → grasshopper → frog → snake → hawk, the grass fixes 1,00,000 J of energy. Assuming the 10 per cent law, how much energy is available to the hawk?

solution.concept: Ten per cent law of energy transfer
solution.explanation: Only about 10% of the energy at one trophic level is transferred to the next. Count the number of transfers from the grass to the hawk.
solution.why_others_wrong: 100 J counts only three transfers (energy reaching the snake). 1000 J is the energy reaching the frog. 1 J counts five transfers.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Ecosystem', energy flow
solution.final_answer: Option C: 10 J

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: Ecological pyramids assume a simple food chain, something that almost never exists in nature, and do not accommodate a food web.
Statement II: Saprophytes are given a separate trophic level at the apex of ecological pyramids.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.explanation: NCERT lists the limitations of ecological pyramids: they do not take into account the same species belonging to two or more trophic levels; they assume a simple food chain and do not accommodate a food web; and saprophytes are not given any place in ecological pyramids even though they play a vital role in the ecosystem.
steps: Statement II: saprophytes have no place in the pyramids → false
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Ecosystem', ecological pyramids
solution.final_answer: Option C: Statement I is true but Statement II is false.

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): In most terrestrial ecosystems, a much larger fraction of energy flows through the detritus food chain than through the grazing food chain.
Reason (R): In an aquatic ecosystem, the grazing food chain is the major conduit for energy flow.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: GFC and DFC in different ecosystems

solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Ecosystem', energy flow: food chains

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text:
Which of the following statements about food chains and trophic levels are correct?

(a) A sparrow is a primary consumer when it eats seeds and fruits, and a secondary consumer when it eats insects and worms.
(b) The number of trophic levels in a grazing food chain is restricted because only about 10 per cent of the energy is transferred from one trophic level to the next.
(c) Decomposers are heterotrophic organisms, mainly fungi and bacteria, that meet their energy and nutrient needs by degrading dead organic matter.
(d) The detritus food chain is not connected to the grazing food chain at any level.
(e) Herbivores are called secondary consumers.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Food chains, food webs and trophic levels
solution.explanation: A species can occupy more than one trophic level at the same time, as the sparrow does. Because only about 10% of energy passes to each higher level, grazing food chains have few trophic levels. Decomposers are saprotrophs, mainly fungi and bacteria. The DFC may be connected with the GFC at some levels (some DFC organisms are prey to GFC animals), forming food webs. Herbivores are primary consumers.
steps: (d) False: the two chains are connected at some levels
solution.why_others_wrong: Options A, B and C each include (d) or (e).
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Ecosystem', energy flow: food chains and food webs
solution.final_answer: Option D: (a), (b) and (c) only

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text: Which of the following is NOT one of the biodiversity hotspots that cover India's regions of exceptionally high biodiversity?

solution.explanation: Of the 34 biodiversity hotspots in the world, three cover India's exceptionally high biodiversity regions: the Western Ghats and Sri Lanka, Indo-Burma, and the Himalaya. The Eastern Ghats are not among them.
steps: India's hotspots: Western Ghats and Sri Lanka; Indo-Burma; Himalaya
solution.why_others_wrong: The other three options are exactly the three hotspots NCERT names.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Biodiversity and Conservation', biodiversity conservation: how do we conserve biodiversity

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text: During his pioneering explorations in the wilderness of South American jungles, who observed that within a region species richness increases with increasing explored area, but only up to a limit?

solution.explanation: The German naturalist and geographer Alexander von Humboldt observed the species–area relationship. On a logarithmic scale it is a straight line: log S = log C + Z log A.
solution.why_others_wrong: Ehrlich proposed the rivet popper hypothesis; Tilman ran long-term ecosystem experiments on stability; Wilson popularised the term biodiversity.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Biodiversity and Conservation', patterns of biodiversity: species-area relationships
solution.final_answer: Option B: Alexander von Humboldt

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text: The introduction of the Nile perch into Lake Victoria in East Africa led to the extinction of more than 200 species of:

solution.explanation: When alien species are introduced, some become invasive and cause decline or extinction of indigenous species. The Nile perch introduced into Lake Victoria eventually led to the extinction of an ecologically unique assemblage of more than 200 species of cichlid fish.
steps: Nile perch in Lake Victoria → loss of >200 cichlid fish species → alien species invasion
solution.why_others_wrong: Catfish is the trap: the threat to indigenous catfishes in Indian rivers comes from the African catfish Clarias gariepinus, a different example.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Biodiversity and Conservation', loss of biodiversity: causes
solution.final_answer: Option D: Cichlid fish

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text: On a logarithmic scale the species–area relationship is a straight line, log S = log C + Z log A. When very large areas such as entire continents are analysed, the slope Z of the line is:

options.text: In the range 0.1 to 0.2, as for any region
Much steeper, in the range 0.6 to 1.2

solution.concept: Regression coefficient Z in the species–area relationship
solution.explanation: For smaller areas, Z values lie in the range 0.1 to 0.2, regardless of the taxonomic group or region. When very large areas such as entire continents are analysed, the slope becomes much steeper, with Z values of 0.6 to 1.2. For frugivorous birds and mammals in the tropical forests of different continents the slope is 1.15.
solution.why_others_wrong: 0.1–0.2 is the usual range for smaller areas. Species richness rises with area, so Z is positive.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Biodiversity and Conservation', patterns of biodiversity: species-area relationships
solution.final_answer: Option B: Much steeper, in the range 0.6 to 1.2

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: Although India has only 2.4 per cent of the world's land area, its share of the global species diversity is an impressive 8.1 per cent.
Statement II: India is one of the 12 megadiversity countries of the world.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.explanation: India has 2.4% of the world's land area but 8.1% of global species diversity, which makes it one of the 12 megadiversity countries. Nearly 45,000 species of plants and twice as many animals have been recorded from India.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Biodiversity and Conservation', biodiversity: how many species are there on earth and how many in India
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): In general, species diversity decreases as we move away from the equator towards the poles.
Reason (R): Tropical environments, unlike temperate ones, are less seasonal, relatively more constant and predictable, which promotes niche specialisation and leads to greater species diversity.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.explanation: Tropics (23.5° N to 23.5° S) harbour more species than temperate or polar areas; for example Colombia has nearly 1400 species of birds while New York has 105 and Greenland 56. One of NCERT's explanations is that tropical environments are less seasonal and more constant and predictable, which promotes niche specialisation and greater diversity. R is one of the accepted reasons for A.
steps: R: true and one of the NCERT explanations for the gradient
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Biodiversity and Conservation', patterns of biodiversity: latitudinal gradients
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text:
Which of the following statements about the causes of biodiversity loss are correct?

(a) Habitat loss and fragmentation is the most important cause driving animals and plants to extinction.
(b) Steller's sea cow and the passenger pigeon became extinct in the last 500 years due to over-exploitation by humans.
(c) The illegal introduction of the African catfish Clarias gariepinus for aquaculture poses a threat to the indigenous catfishes of our rivers.
(d) When a host fish species becomes extinct, its unique assemblage of parasites also meets the same fate.
(e) Parthenium, Lantana and water hyacinth are native Indian species threatened by over-exploitation.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.explanation: The four major causes of biodiversity loss are habitat loss and fragmentation (the most important), over-exploitation, alien species invasions and co-extinctions. Parthenium (carrot grass), Lantana and water hyacinth (Eichhornia) are invasive alien weeds that threaten native species; they are not native species threatened by over-exploitation.
steps: (e) False: they are invasive alien weeds
solution.why_others_wrong: Options B, C and D include (e).
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Biodiversity and Conservation', loss of biodiversity: causes
solution.final_answer: Option A: (a), (b), (c) and (d) only

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: David Tilman's long-term ecosystem experiments using outdoor plots showed that plots with more species had less year-to-year variation in total biomass.
Statement II: The 'rivet popper' hypothesis, which compares species in an ecosystem to the rivets of an airplane, was proposed by David Tilman.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.explanation: Tilman found that plots with more species showed less year-to-year variation in total biomass and that increased diversity contributed to higher productivity. The rivet popper hypothesis was proposed by the Stanford ecologist Paul Ehrlich: losing rivets (species) on key parts such as the wings is a more serious threat than losing a few on the seats.
steps: Statement II: proposed by Paul Ehrlich, not Tilman → false
solution.why_others_wrong: Both ideas are about stability and come from the same NCERT section, which makes the swap of names easy to miss.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Biodiversity and Conservation', importance of species diversity to the ecosystem
solution.final_answer: Option C: Statement I is true but Statement II is false.

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): All the biodiversity hotspots of the world put together cover less than 2 per cent of the earth's land area.
Reason (R): Biodiversity hotspots are identified on the basis of very high levels of species richness and a high degree of endemism.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.explanation: Hotspots are regions with very high species richness and a high degree of endemism. Together they cover less than 2% of the earth's land area, yet the number of species they harbour is extremely high, and strict protection of them could reduce ongoing mass extinctions by almost 30%. The criteria in R define what a hotspot is; they do not explain why the hotspots together occupy so small an area.
steps: R gives the criteria, not the reason for the small total area → B
solution.why_others_wrong: Option A is the trap: R is the definition of a hotspot, which does not account for their total area.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Biodiversity and Conservation', biodiversity conservation: hotspots
solution.final_answer: Option B: Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Botany
questions.subtopic: In situ and ex situ conservation
questions.question_text:
Which of the following statements about conservation of biodiversity are correct?

(a) Biosphere reserves, national parks and wildlife sanctuaries are means of in situ conservation.
(b) Zoological parks, botanical gardens and wildlife safari parks are means of ex situ conservation.
(c) Preserving gametes of threatened species by cryopreservation is a method of in situ conservation.
(d) Sacred groves are found in the Khasi and Jaintia Hills of Meghalaya.
(e) Seed banks conserve plants in their natural habitat.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: In situ and ex situ conservation
solution.explanation: In situ (on site) conservation protects the whole ecosystem: biosphere reserves, national parks, wildlife sanctuaries and sacred groves (Khasi and Jaintia Hills, Aravalli Hills, Western Ghats, Sarguja, Chanda and Bastar). Ex situ (off site) conservation removes threatened species from their habitat: zoological parks, botanical gardens, wildlife safari parks, cryopreservation of gametes, and seed banks.
steps: (e) False: seed banks store seeds away from the habitat (ex situ)
solution.why_others_wrong: Options A, B and D include (c) or (e), both ex situ methods described as in situ.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Biodiversity and Conservation', biodiversity conservation: in situ and ex situ conservation
solution.final_answer: Option C: (a), (b) and (d) only
